status_key.N: No source. The memo states it but names no source, or only says 'task anchor', 'snippet' or 'reviews'.
status_key.C: Conflicts. A source we have read points the other way, or the cited study does.
status_key.W: Weak source. A source is named, but only its abstract, a search summary or a page extract was read.
status_key.S: Secondary. A review or standard we read in full states it and names the primary study; the primary is not read.
status_key.V: Verified. The primary source was read in full.

new_sources.read: Read in full on 2026-11-05 from the Apify pull (raw/text/326-html.txt).

new_sources.name: EFSA 2023, Welfare of broilers on farm, EFSA Journal 21(2):7788
new_sources.read: Section 3.4.2.12 read in full on 2026-11-05, from raw/pdf/212.pdf. new_sources.name: Riber et al. 2021, Post-mortem examination of fast-growing broilers with different degrees of identifiable gait defects, Veterinary Record, doi 10.1002/vetr.454
new_sources.read: Author proof read in full on 2026-11-06 by a subagent; Table 2 re-checked from the page image.

scenarios.title: Growth rate and breed choice

claims.t: Welfare load tracks the peak daily gain (about 100 g/day in week 5), not the lifetime average.
claims.src: Units note in the biology memo; no source.

claims.t: Pushing a strain with higher-energy feed adds harm on top of the breed choice.
Breed is the highest-leverage welfare lever; fixes further down are second-best.
claims.src: EFSA 2023 section 3.6 concludes that broiler health and welfare mainly depend on genetics; its Table 8 makes genetics the top hazard (10 of 19 welfare consequences). EFSA does not rank the other levers as second-best.

claims.t: About 50 g/day average gain is the welfare cap.
claims.src: EFSA 2023 recommends a 50 g/day maximum, quoted in RSPCA-J.

claims.t: Fast breeds have more leg, heart and contact-dermatitis problems and die or are culled more.
claims.src: RSPCA-J, citing Bailie 2018, Dixon 2020, Rayner 2020, Wijesurendra 2017.

claims.t: Going from 50 to 58 g/day triples mortality (2.1% to 6.2%), doubles hock burn, and raises footpad lesions from 0% to 7%.
A fast breed at 34 kg/m2 is the worst combination tested.

gaps: No estimate of how much pain, for how long, fast growth adds per bird. The Welfare Footprint Project's broiler work was never pulled.

scenarios.title: Ascites (fluid in the belly from heart failure)

claims.t: Cold in the first three weeks raises ascites risk.
Cobb birds are the most susceptible strain and Ross the least.
Growth rate matters more than ventilation or vitamin C fixes.
More than 2% of flocks are affected at baseline.
Up to about 25% of a flock under challenge; fast birds about 35% more prone.
claims.src: Baghbanzadeh and Decuypere 2008; blocked, search summary only.

claims.t: Rearing above 900 m altitude is unsatisfactory.
Divergent selection lines: 93.9% versus 9.5% ascites.
Fast breeds are more at risk of heart and circulation disease.

gaps: What ascites feels like for the bird and for how long; no source on its welfare cost.

scenarios.title: Sudden death syndrome (flip-over)

claims.t: 60 to 80% of sudden-death birds are males.
Carnitine or electrolyte additives do not solve it.
It is often recorded as general mortality, so it is under-counted.
0.5 to 4% of a flock, peaking at 2 to 4 weeks.
Much lower with low-density feed and slower early growth.

gaps: Death is fast, so suffering per bird may be brief. The memo does not weigh this.

scenarios.title: Leg disorders (tibial dyschondroplasia, valgus-varus, femoral head necrosis)

claims.t: Tibial dyschondroplasia affects about 30% of broilers in general and about 22% at 6 weeks.
claims.src: The 22% is Shi 2024's 6-week rate in Chinese yellow-feathered cockerels (X-ray), not a commercial white broiler. Dinev 2012 review (read in full) gives 24 to 28% at necropsy in Ross 308, Cobb 500 and Pureline, first lesions at about 24 days (citing unpublished data). 'About 30%' is only a secondary citation. 04-leg-disorders/verified.md

claims.t: Valgus-varus (angled legs) affects about 5.4% at 5 weeks.
claims.src: Tang 2020 and Chen 2022 (read in full) state 0.4% at 1 week rising to 5.4% at 5 weeks, citing Cruickshank and Sim 1986 (abstract only). Riber 2021 (read in full): 5.0% in Ross 308 at 38 days. Counting mild angles gives much more: valgus 30 to 40% in Leterrier and Nys 1992 (abstract). 04-leg-disorders/verified.md

claims.t: Femoral head necrosis and bacterial chondronecrosis rise from about 1% to 13.3% at high density, up to about 20%.
claims.src: No source for a density rise. 13.3% is the share of BCO lesions culturing E. coli or mixed bacteria (Thorp 1993, via Dinev 2012); 20% traces to a human hip-fracture paper. The ~1% fits McNamee and Smyth 2000 (abstract): 0.75% of male birds placed. 04-leg-disorders/verified.md

claims.t: Many lesions are hidden until necropsy, so gait scores understate the lesion load.
claims.src: Riber 2021 (author proof read in full): 15 of 19 normally walking (GS0) birds had a leg pathology at necropsy, 9 of 19 femoral head necrosis; no difference by gait score (P = 0.23). Fernandes 2012 (read in full) agrees. 04-leg-disorders/verified.md

claims.t: Fast versus slow strains at 6 weeks: valgus scores 0.40/0.38 versus 0.26/0.28; tibial dyschondroplasia 0.06 versus 0.02.
claims.src: Shim 2012; abstract. These are mean lesion scores, not prevalences, and the abstract gives 6 weeks for TD only. Full text is behind a bot check.

claims.t: Fast-growing breeds are more prone to leg disorders.
Some leg disorders are painful, and lame birds also go thirsty and hungry when they cannot reach feed and water.
claims.src: EFSA 2023 section 3.4.2.12, citing Hothersall 2016 and Weeks 2000. Analgesic studies (McGeown 1999, Danbury 2000, Caplen 2013a, Hothersall 2016) hold at abstract level, all in moderately or more lame birds; none tests subclinical TD, valgus-varus or gait score 1 to 2. 04-leg-disorders/verified.md

claims.t: Risk factors: genotype, growth rate, body shape, diet, wet litter, high density, low activity, infection.

Lameness pain, modelled: an average fast-growing bird has about 54 hours of Disabling pain from lameness versus about 16 in a slower breed; gait score 3 begins at 10 to 31 days in fast birds; unculled birds that stop eating and drinking take 5 to 25 days to die.
claims.src: WFP-BROILER-CH2, read in full. The onset windows are the authors' assumptions; they say no data on lameness progression exist. 04-leg-disorders/verified.md

claims.t: Clinical BCO: losses of 0.75% of male birds placed; present in 17.3% of lame birds; cases from 14 to 70 days, most around 35; visible to the naked eye in only 40 to 67% of cases.
Higher stocking density worsens gait and footpad and hock burns but did not change tibial dyschondroplasia or hock angulation.
Lame birds lie 86% of the time versus 76% for sound birds, and eat lying down for almost half their feeding time.

gaps: Measured (not modelled) duration of lameness per bird; the WFP chapter says no progression data exist.
EFSA 2023 section 3.6 adds that lame birds may stay at the feeder, skip the drinker, dehydrate and sometimes die of it (no primary cited).
Four sources need Arda at the browser: Shim 2012 (ScienceDirect bot check), Leterrier and Nys 1992 and McNamee and Smyth 2000 (Taylor and Francis), the Animal Biotechnology 2023 leg-disorders review.
New options to weigh: early feed restriction, dark periods from day 4, prompt culling of gait score 4 and 5 birds, hatchery incubation profile. See 04-leg-disorders/adjudicated.md.
leads: Cobb-hosted Sluis 2022 paper on early activity and leg health (raw/pdf/064.pdf), not read.

scenarios.title: Breast myopathies (woody breast, white striping)

claims.t: Woody breast hurts or impairs the living bird. This is the welfare claim itself.
claims.src: No source; the memo calls it muscle necrosis.

claims.t: Severe woody breast rises sharply above about 2.7 kg live weight.
It cannot be processed away, only bred or grown away.
Woody breast odds 1.75 times higher above 78 g/day gain.
Woody breast odds 1.23 times higher at 2.46 to 2.63 kg.
Severe woody breast 24.2% in Ross 708 versus 4.7% in Ranger Gold.
Four strains: severe woody breast 5, 35, 5 and 16%.
Males 25.2% versus females 12.1%.
High-energy diets worsen white striping.
White striping odds rise with breast weight and genotype.
Lesions start at 2 weeks; a 1950s line shows almost none.

leads: Aviagen broiler myopathy handbook 2023 (raw/pdf/016.pdf), not read.

claims.t: Higher density adds heat load.
claims.src: EFSA 2023 section 3.4.2.9, citing Najafi 2015 and de Jong 2012a: more heat is produced and it dissipates less well at high density.

claims.t: Lower density makes birds use enrichment more.
Gait score worsens by 0.013 per kg/m2.
Density is a weak lever per unit: a 0.24 gait gain needs an 18.5 kg/m2 cut.
Above 30 kg/m2 birds are crowded, can't move freely and are disturbed while resting; they climb a high barrier to escape crowding.
Above 11 kg/m2 footpad lesions rise and walking and natural behaviour suffer.
Different outcomes worsen over different density ranges; no single threshold.
claims.src: Buijs 2009, abstract. EFSA 2023 instead sets one combined limit of 11 kg/m2, and its elicited no-effect densities for walking (median 12.3) and footpad dermatitis (median 10.1) nearly coincide (Appendix B, Tables B.6 and B.11).

claims.t: From 30 to 39 kg/m2: footpad score 1.13 to 1.26, litter moisture up 3.1 points, ammonia up.
Management mattered for 17 of 19 welfare measures; density for 3.
Darkness helps legs mainly by cutting feeding time and slowing growth.
claims.src: Memo, no source. RSPCA-J instead links short dark periods to strain from activity, and says 'presumably'.

claims.t: Dim light around 5 lux harms eyes and activity.
claims.src: EFSA 2023 section 3.5.1.4, citing Blatchford 2009 and Rault 2017: at 5 lux birds were less active and had heavier eyes, but leg health did not differ. The clearer harm is at 1 lux (Deep 2010).

claims.t: Gait score improves by 0.079 per hour of darkness.
A clear day and night gives rest; 7 to 8 hours of dark is best for welfare.
Longer dark periods go with more content, active flocks.
Natural light raises activity, improves gait and is preferred by the birds.
At least 50 lux raises activity without cutting gain; 4 hours unbroken dark is needed for eye development.
claims.src: BCC white paper, citing Blatchford 2009, Deep 2013, Li 2000.

claims.t: 38-day mortality 3.33, 3.74, 4.97 and 6.11% at 14, 17, 20 and 23 hours of light.
23 hours of light enlarges eyes and worsens gait.

scenarios.title: Litter and footpad dermatitis

claims.t: Footpad lesions are painful; birds with severe lesions grow slower, probably from pain.
claims.src: RSPCA-J, citing Schulze Kersting 1996 and Martland 1985.

claims.t: Ammonia irritates eyes and airways; birds avoid more than 10 ppm when given a choice.
Wood shavings and peat cause less footpad dermatitis than straw.
Litter above about 30% moisture causes damage.
claims.src: EFSA 2023 section 3.5.1.6 puts ideal litter dry matter above 75% (moisture under about 25%), with no primary cited, and gives no 30% figure. de Jong not read.

claims.t: Wet versus dry litter: footpad score 2.92 versus 0.70 at day 42, starting about 14 days earlier.
Each 3.1 points more moisture adds 0.13 to the footpad score.

gaps: Realism: whether farms really cull or wash feet to game the slaughter-line footpad score is unsourced.

claims.t: String is a cheap enrichment that raises foraging.
claims.src: BCC paper (Bailie 2015, 2018). RSPCA-J advises against string because birds can swallow it.

claims.t: Broilers sit 70 to 80% of the time as they get heavy.
claims.src: EFSA 2023 Appendix C: median sitting 56.9% of scans across 17 studies (range 24.9 to 81.9%), not split by age. Section 3.5.1.4: 61% resting at 6 weeks (Kristensen 2006).

claims.t: Enrichment cannot overcome a heavy fast bird's unwillingness to move.
Straw bales and perches lower hock burn and footpad lesions and raise activity.
claims.src: RSPCA-J, citing CIWF 2013 and Bailie and Weeks 2013.

claims.t: More types of enrichment plus more space give better welfare.
Platforms improve gait and reduce tibial dyschondroplasia.
One study found enrichment did not improve leg health in either breed.

scenarios.title: Gait scoring and culling lame birds

claims.t: Triage: keep gait score 0 to 2, assess score 3, cull score 4 to 5.
claims.src: Memo. RSPCA requires culling at score 3 or more. EFSA 2023 (sections 3.10.2 and 4.2.5.1, citing Weeks 2000) sets the line at gait score 4: sick pen or cull.

claims.t: At 40 days, 27.6% of birds score 3 or more and 3.3% score 4 or more.
Flock gait scores do not match recorded leg culls.
Birds at score 3 or more are in pain; lame birds choose feed with a painkiller in it.
Lame birds go thirsty and hungry when they cannot reach the lines.
Manual neck dislocation raises welfare concerns; neck-crushing pliers are not humane.
claims.src: RSPCA-J, citing Gregory and Wotton 1990, Erasmus 2010, Hopkins 2015.

scenarios.title: Breeder feed restriction level

claims.t: How much welfare feeding above the target weight curve buys, and at what fertility cost.
claims.src: EFSA 2023 section 3.7.2.4: a 10% higher growth trajectory reduced feeding motivation without harming health or reproduction (Afrouziyeh 2021). EFSA recommends at least 10% more feed than the breeder guidelines.

claims.t: RSPCA's growth cap exists partly to protect parent birds; the JA757 female line needed little or no restriction.
In rearing, birds get 25 to 33% of what they would eat, most severely from weeks 6 to 16.
claims.src: de Jong and van Emous 2017 chapter, citing De Jong 2002.

claims.t: In lay, 45 to 80% of free intake up to peak and about 80% after.
EFSA 2010 ranked the restricted diet the top welfare hazard for breeders.
Feeding to appetite causes obesity, laying disorders and shorter fertility.
claims.src: EFSA 2023 section 3.6, citing Hocking 1990, 1996 and 2002: obesity, heart and leg problems and reduced fertility. Laying disorders are not named.

leads: Ross 308 parent-stock Performance Objectives 2021, the week-by-week table the memo could not get (raw/pdf/018.pdf, 019.pdf), not read.

claims.t: Skip-a-day feeding is worse for welfare on the off days.
claims.src: No source, and Morrissey 2014 (search) found no difference in rearing hunger. EFSA 2023 section 3.7.2.4 finds the evidence mixed (Arrazola 2019a and 2020 less feeding motivation in rearing, 2019b more at end of lay; Morrissey 2014 no decrease) and section 4.2.2.2 does not recommend skip-a-day, citing health and production.

claims.t: A daily diluted ration with foraging litter is the least bad option.
Fibre diets cut damaging pecking and stereotypies, but some worsen litter.
Stress hormone did not differ between diets; roughage helped and sugar-beet pulp hurt.
claims.src: EFSA 2023 section 3.7.2.4, citing Tahamtani and Riber 2020 (roughage helped; soluble fibre caused a sickness feeling), Aranibar 2020 and van Emous 2014 (corticosterone unchanged). Sugar-beet pulp is not named.

scenarios.title: Appetite suppressants sold as welfare

claims.t: High-fibre bulk, like calcium propionate, may cut eating by making birds feel unwell.
claims.src: EFSA 2023 section 3.7.2.4: calcium propionate (Arrazola 2019a) and soluble fibre (Tahamtani and Riber 2020) cause a sickness feeling, but at least 10% insoluble fibre reduces hunger without harm (section 4.2.2.1). High-fibre bulk as a group is not the problem.

claims.t: Birds learn to avoid a place paired with calcium propionate (8% to 58.7%).
claims.src: Arrazola and Torrey 2019; page extract. EFSA 2023 section 3.7.2.4 confirms the avoidance (Arrazola 2019a) but gives no figures.

claims.t: Researchers suspected since 1993 that suppressants work by making birds ill.

gaps: Realism: whether US breeder farms use calcium propionate at all.

claims.t: Evidence from motivation tests outweighs hormone evidence.
Restricted birds peck at objects, over-drink and pace.
Stress hormone and the heterophil-to-lymphocyte ratio rise under restriction.
Restricted birds pay 2 to 3 times more to reach an empty foraging area.
Those hormones may only reflect low energy, not suffering.
claims.src: EFSA 2023 section 3.7.2.4: corticosterone tracks metabolic rate, so a raised level is not a good stress indicator (de Jong 2002).

claims.t: No reliable behavioural hunger test exists.

scenarios.title: Breeder male aggression, mating ratio and spiking

claims.t: Swapping males within a farm raises aggression for about 2 weeks without raising deaths.
How much forced mating injures and frightens hens.
claims.src: EFSA 2023 section 3.4.2.19: often severe and affects most females; fear, pain, plumage loss and wounds (Millman 2000; de Jong 2009). No injury rates.

claims.t: How painful toe-clipping, de-spurring and beak trimming are.
claims.src: EFSA 2023 section 3.8.1: beak trimming is painful (Gentle and McKeegan 2007), and toe clipping left neuromas 60 days later (Gentle and Hunter 1988). No measure of how much pain.

claims.t: Over-mating signs appear from about week 26; the remedy is removing males.
Breeder males are more aggressive and court less; the cause is genetic, not feed restriction.
Lower density and separating the sexes 5 hours a day improve mating and feather cover.
claims.src: Chapter, citing De Jong 2011 and van Emous 2010.

claims.t: Adding new males brings disease and aggression risk.
Mating is 5 to 10 times more frequent than in nature.

scenarios.title: Feed withdrawal before slaughter

claims.t: Contamination risk is U-shaped, so 8 to 12 hours off feed is best for both food safety and welfare.
claims.src: Snippet. RSPCA-J quotes EFSA 2004a: no definitive food-safety evidence for any fasting time.

claims.t: How fast hunger and thirst build up per hour without feed.
Broilers' high metabolism means long fasts harm them; RSPCA caps fasting at 10 hours.
Birds lose 0.23 to 0.33% of body weight per hour off feed.
Gut strength falls after about 14 hours.

leads: Purdue AS-576 feed withdrawal guide (raw/pdf/271.pdf), not read.

scenarios.title: Stunning method at slaughter

claims.t: Inert-gas stunning (argon or nitrogen) is about as good as two-phase CO2.
Birds lose consciousness in about 20 seconds in gas.
Low-current, high-frequency waterbath stuns risk birds waking before or during bleeding.
EU minimum currents: 100, 150 and 200 mA per chicken by frequency band.
Neck cut within 10 seconds (high frequency) or 15 seconds (50 Hz).
Shackling causes pain and distress, and wing flapping causes dislocations and fractures.
Waterbaths give some birds shocks before the stun, and some are not stunned.
CO2 is aversive from about 25%, more so above 40%; a gradual rise gives a calmer induction.

leads: Red Tractor stunning and killing methods (raw/pdf/241.pdf); Cobb processing guide (065.pdf). Not read.

scenarios.title: Catching and loading

claims.t: Carrying birds upside down or by one leg is what drives bruising, dislocations and heat deaths.
claims.src: No source; the memo calls it 'the robust effect'.

claims.t: In fast broilers the main injury shifts from fractures (as in hens) to bruising and dislocations.
A recent field study found dead-on-arrival 0.16% after machine catching versus 0.06% by hand.
Hand versus machine catching: small, inconsistent differences in injuries and deaths.
claims.src: Ekstrand 1998, Knierim and Gocke 2003, Delezie 2006; search summaries.

claims.t: Loading above 30 C makes dead-on-arrival 16.89 times higher; freezing plus high humidity adds 43%.
Mean dead-on-arrival about 0.08% in Britain and 0.46% in the Netherlands and Germany.
Journeys over 4 hours: 0.28% mortality versus 0.16% under 4 hours.

gaps: Fear and stress of being caught, separate from injury.
leads: Red Tractor catching and transport standards (262.pdf); Eyes on Animals catching report (266.pdf); Aviagen pre-processing handling note (035.pdf); BroilerNet catching-team training (261.pdf). Not read.

scenarios.title: Emergency depopulation in a disease outbreak

claims.t: How long and how badly birds suffer under ventilation shutdown plus heat or CO2.
claims.src: No source; AAAP ranks methods but gives no welfare data.

claims.t: How foam compares with CO2 in what the bird goes through.
Foam and gassing are preferred for floor birds; shutdown alone is not recommended.
Foam must reach 1 ft above the birds' heads; shutdown-plus must kill all birds within 1.5 hours.
Foam is not recommended for caged birds, so the ranking flips from hens.

leads: AAAP depopulation FAQ (196.pdf); USAHA welfare resolutions (195.pdf, 199.pdf). Not read.

scenarios.title: Thinning (removing part of the flock early)

claims.t: There is no welfare-correct thinning.
claims.src: Memo. EFSA 2023 suggests lowering density 'e.g. by thinning' when litter cannot be kept dry. The full read finds EFSA endorsing thinning in several more places (heat stress, movement, foraging, group stress) without weighing the cost of the thinning catch.

claims.t: Thinned flocks have worse gait (plus 0.25) beyond what age explains.
Thinning stresses the birds left behind: feed and water taken away, noise, forklifts, injuries and temperature swings.
The birds left behind reach maximum density twice.

gaps: Food-safety claims (Campylobacter doubles) are not counted here; their best source is 'Finland research cited by University of Bristol', via RSPCA-J.
